Chapter 4: Embracing Impermanence and Finding Freedom in Change.
You know, change really is the only constant in life. But isn’t it funny how it's also the one thing most of us push back against? There’s this deep wish for everything to stay just as it is—for relationships, our health, our happiness—to somehow be frozen in time.
But life? It has other plans. Seasons shift, we grow older, and circumstances keep evolving, whether we want them to or not.
That resistance to change... it’s a huge source of suffering. Our minds latch onto what feels safe and familiar, afraid of losing it or facing the unknown. But the tighter we hold on, the more it hurts when things inevitably slip away. It’s kind of like grabbing a handful of sand—the harder you squeeze, the faster it runs out between your fingers.
Picture a couple, just married, full of hope. They dream up a perfect future, create plans, and hope for smooth sailing. But as years go by, life throws curveballs—illness, job loss, disagreements. The dream starts to blur. At first, there’s frustration, even grief. But as they adjust, they discover something beautiful. Their love deepens, not because everything went perfectly, but because they learned how to grow together through all the changes.
What most people don’t see right away is that impermanence isn’t out to get us. It’s actually one of life’s greatest teachers. It reminds us how precious every moment really is. After all, if nothing ever changed, how could we grow? How could we discover anything new? The things we treasure most—love, creativity, connection—they’re only possible because life keeps moving.
Think about all the messages we get from the world around us. There’s this push to ignore impermanence—to chase youth, pile up achievements, collect more and more stuff. The idea is: just hold on tight to what’s good and steer clear of the bad. But that mindset? It only leads to disappointment and fear. So when change finally comes, it feels like something went wrong. When really, it’s just life doing what it does.
Letting go of the need for things to stay the same—it takes courage. It means being willing to face the unknown, to accept loss, and to welcome new possibilities. It's not about giving up. It's about joining in with the flow of life. When we stop fighting change, there’s a real sense of freedom—a weight lifts, because we’re not struggling to control the uncontrollable.
Imagine a musician improvising on stage. They don’t know what note is coming next. There’s risk, sure—but also excitement. The music feels alive precisely because it’s unpredictable. If every note were planned, the magic would disappear. Life is the same way. Its richness comes from not knowing exactly what’s around the corner.
For most of us, it’s through difficult times that we realize: clinging to the past, or worrying about the future, just adds to our pain. When we accept the present—changes and all—something shifts. The mind settles, the heart opens, and everything feels more vivid, more alive.
Of course, this doesn’t mean loss or change is ever easy. Grief, disappointment, fear—they’re all very real. But they’re also a part of being human. When we meet these feelings with compassion, instead of resistance, they can actually help us grow.
Picture a teacher, getting ready to retire. There’s sadness in letting go, but also deep gratitude for what’s been. The future is uncertain, but there’s a quiet trust that new adventures are waiting. In that acceptance, there’s a kind of gentle joy—a sense that, even though nothing lasts forever, every moment truly matters.
Embracing impermanence isn’t about giving up. It’s about living fully, right here and now. It’s an invitation to join in the dance of life—to find meaning, not in what we cling to, but in what we experience. Real freedom doesn’t come from certainty, but from the willingness to show up for whatever life brings.
